power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Spoken communica on is largely defined by its transience.

This must be done rapidly; speakers produce words roughly three to five mes per second, placing significant demands on listeners to comprehend speech quickly or risk losing access to informa on that is cri cal for understanding a message.

Research in spoken word recogni on has converged on mechanisms by which this is accomplished (by typical listeners under standardized listening condi ons): Immediately a er the onset of a word is heard (e.g., the ini al /fl/ when hearing flick) listeners consider mul ple lexical candidates as reasonable parses of the signal (flick, flip, flea, flat, flack etc.).

They then reassess these candidates con nuously as informa on arrives (only flick remains a er the final /k/ is heard; Allopenna et al., 1998; Grosjean, 1980; Marslen-Wilson, 1987; Marslen-Wilson & Zwitserlood, 1989).

text.text: The high sensi vity of the system to its input thus allows for efficiency without sacrificing accuracy.
However, recent work has found that this is not the only form that the dynamics of compe on can take.

For instance, some listeners with hearing loss show delayed processing; instead of immediately ac va ng lexical candidates word recogni on is delayed for several hundred milliseconds (Klein et al., 2023; McMurray et al., 2017; McMurray et al., 2024).

text.text: This suggests that word recogni on changes in response to both chronic, long-term ontogene c factors (like hearing loss or a language disorder) and to local, acute changes to immediate challenge in the signal.

Understanding the factors that ul mately shape the nature of word recogni on in challenge may provide insight into a common problem in hearing science: Listeners, especially those with hearing loss, show high degrees of variability in their ability to understand speech in challenging condi ons.

Research has found that this is due in part to hearing acuity and other peripheral auditory factors (Fu & Nogaki, 2005; Fu et al., 1998; Kaandorp et al., 2017) and in part due to general cogni ve factors (Amini et al., 2024; Ching et al., 2018; O'Neill et al., 2019; Zaltz et al., 2020).

text.text: It could be that the specific way that the mechanisms of spoken word recogni on adapt to challenge explains some of this variability.

Suppor ng this, work with CI users finds that the degree to which they delay recogni on or maintain candidates predicts speech in noise performance (both being associated with worse outcomes; McMurray et al., 2024).

text.text: Here, we examine three main ques ons regarding the nature of change in spoken word recogni on in challenge: (I) to what degree is a listener's response to challenge constrained by how they perform in standard condi ons; (II) are responses to challenge stable across me; and (III) do individual differences in these changes predict speech percep on outcomes in challenging condi ons?
We describe our approach to each of these ques ons below.

Compe on among lexical candidates has been studied using ga ng (Grosjean, 1980) and cross-modal priming (Luce & Cluff, 1998; Marslen-Wilson & Zwitserlood, 1989), but modern approaches typically use the Visual World Paradigm (VWP; Allopenna et al., 1998; Tanenhaus et al., 1995).

text.text: In this task, listener's eyes are tracked as they locate and select a referent of a spoken word (the target flea) from among four pictured alterna ves.
These are chosen to test hypotheses about which words are considered in conjunc on with the target.

For instance, displayed alongside flea might be referents for the words fleece (which overlaps at onset, referred to as a cohort) or glee (a rhyme), along with a baseline referent that is not phone cally related.

The fixa ons that listeners make to these referents over me can reveal when, and how much, listeners consider each as a reasonable interpreta on of the signal as the input (and their decision) unfolds over me.
The standard pa ern of results is that early in processing listeners will look at the target and words that share its onset (commonly referred to as cohort compe tors) about equally.
At later points (a er more of the input has unfolded), they stop looking to the cohort but may begin looking to the rhyme (as this later por on of the input matches rhymes but rules out cohorts).
Importantly, looks to both cohort and rhyme compe tors exceed looks to phone cally unrelated referents, sugges ng these fixa ons are language-directed (Salverda et al., 2011).

text.text: Remarkably, though a range of popula ons and listening condi ons have been tested, listeners seem to consistently show one of two profiles.
First, in some cases lexical access is delayed en rely even as speech input con nues to arrive.
The obvious result of this is that looks to the target image are delayed.

Less obvious though is that this also results in reduced looks to the cohort, as recogni on does not begin un l later informa on in the word has arrived, at which me there is more evidence to rule out cohorts.
Similarly, rhymes may be increased because the ini al informa on needed to rule them out has come and gone (Figure 1).

text.text: This profile has been given the colloquial term Wait-and-See.

Cochlear implant users who received their implant at a young age demonstrate such a profile in non-noisy, quiet condi ons (McMurray et al., 2017) as do normal hearing adults listening to heavily degraded (McMurray et al., 2017) or extremely quiet speech (Hendrickson & Ernest, 2022; Hendrickson et al., 2020).

text.text: Second, the ming of recogni on may remain rela vely unchanged, but looks to compe tors are not fully suppressed-listeners instead maintain looks to the cohort or rhyme compe tors even a er they have commi ed to the target (Figure 1).

text.text: This Sustained Ac va on has been observed in cochlear implant users who received their implant at later ages (Farris-Trimble et al., 2014) and in normal hearing adults listening to noise-masked speech (Ben-David et al., 2011; Brouwer & Bradlow, 2015; Farris-Trimble et al., 2014).

text.text: (Interes ngly, it also seems to occur in listeners with exposure to mul ple dialects; Clopper & Walker, 2017).

text.text: Wait-and-See and Sustained Ac va on have each been observed in dis nct experiments and with dis nct popula ons or listening condi ons.
This suggests they may be mutually exclusive-people demonstrate one or the other depending on the condi oning factor.
However, most of these prior studies focused on group-level trends and inves gated a single listening factor (e.g., cochlear implants vs. normal hearing) or condi on (noise vs. quiet).
This raises the possibility that these are not truly independent.

Indeed, recent work has discovered that these are in fact orthogonal dimensions which underly spoken word recogni on across types of listeners and listening condi ons (McMurray et al., 2024; Muegge & McMurray, 2025).
text.formatted: Indeed, recent work has discovered that these are in fact orthogonal dimensions which underly spoken word recogni on across types of listeners and listening condi ons <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(McMurray et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Muegge & McMurray, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: That is, listeners primarily differ from one another in the degree to which they delay recogni on and/or maintain candidates, with any individual's profile of word recogni on reflec ng some mix of both.
The work which first demonstrated this used a Principal Components Analysis (PCA) to find underlying structure in the dynamics of word recogni on across listeners (McMurray et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The work which first demonstrated this used a Principal Components Analysis (PCA) to find underlying structure in the dynamics of word recogni on across listeners <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(McMurray et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The authors tested a large popula on of highly variable CI users and age-matched NH listeners in a VWP task in quiet (i.e., no noise-masking or degrada on).
Note that for the CI users, even though the speech was clear, the CI typically imposes a fair amount of degrada on on the signal, meaning that it was s ll fairly challenging for this group.
The authors then fit each listener's fixa ons over me with non-linear func ons.
The parameters of these func ons served as high-dimensional descrip ons of the mecourse of recogni on for each listener.
When submi ed to a PCA, these parameters were reduced to five meaningful Principal Components (PCs) which collec vely accounted for 80.6% of the variance.

These PCs were then iden fied by examining the loadings of the parameters and via a visualiza on procedure in which these loadings were used to reinterpret what each dimension would look like as eye-tracking data.

The first two PCs reflected Wait-and-See and Sustained Ac va on (accoun ng for 28.6% and 21.5% of the variance, respec vely); the first was strongly associated with later looks to the target and the second was associated with elevated looks to the cohort at the end of processing.
This suggests that variance in the dynamics of lexical access in these listeners can be broadly defined by a listeners' degree of Sustained-Ac va on and Wait-and-See.
But cri cally, each listener (including the NH listeners) adopted their own unique blend of these two profiles.

It is worth no ng that this is rather unexpected; the PCA did not need to have found dimensions which were interpretable, to say nothing of components which reflected well-known (and wellstudied) profiles of word recogni on.
Moreover, since a PCA by defini on discovers orthogonal dimensions, this suggests that listeners can independently vary in their degree of delay and maintenance.
This does not necessarily imply mutual exclusivity-listeners can show high Waitand-See and low Sustained Ac va on (and vice versa), or high values of both.

Given that CI users and NH listeners in challenge demonstrate similar profiles of recogni on at a group level (Farris-Trimble et al., 2014; McMurray et al., 2017), and that CI users demonstrate Wait-and-See and Sustained Ac va on as underlying dimensions, a reasonable conclusion is the NH listeners in challenge would also show these dimensions.

text.text: This is not a given, however.

Variance in performance may be very different for listeners who experience chronic exposure to challenge rela ve to those who only experience it intermi ently. Muegge and McMurray (2025) addressed these ques ons by tes ng NH listeners in two types of challenging listening condi ons (noise masking and vocoding, a type of signal degrada on).

text.text: They found that Wait-and-See and Sustained Ac va on again cons tuted the two most important dimensions (~50% of the variance).
Cri cally, these appeared as the most important dimensions for a PCA conducted on each challenge-type separately and again when pooled across challenge types.
This argues that NH listeners in all kinds of challenge are defined by the same dimensions as CI users.
Since the same listeners were tested in both condi ons, Muegge and McMurray (2025) could also ask whether (and how) responses changed as a func on of different types of listening challenge.

They found that listeners were largely stable: A listener's "loca on" (in the twodimensional Sustained Ac va on  Wait-and-See space) was correlated (r = 0.56 for the Waitand-See dimension; r = 0.32 for Sustained Ac va on).
This suggests that listeners who showed Sustained Ac va on in vocoding also generally showed Sustained Ac va on in noise.

Importantly, however, these loca ons were not iden cal; listeners increased Sustained Ac va on when hearing vocoded speech (rela ve to speech in noise), though they showed no change in the degree of Wait-and-See across condi ons.

This suggests that Wait-and-See might be a more stable property (perhaps a result of long-term developmental pressures) while Sustained Ac va on may be more malleable to in-the-moment demands, but crucially that the level of each is consistent across challenge types.
The strong correla on for each dimension across condi ons raises the ques on of whether listeners are more broadly constrained by their baseline performance.

That is, it may be that the typical way listeners recognize words (the rela vely small degree to which they demonstrate Wait-and-See and Sustained Ac va on in quiet) strongly restricts how they recognize words in challenge.
This would explain why listeners are stable across condi ons; they are anchored to a sub-region of processing space, and thus their responses to various types of challenge are necessarily similar.
In contrast, listeners might be unconstrained by their baseline profile of recogni on.

In light of the prior correla ons for Wait-and-See and Sustained Ac va on, this would suggest that listeners might dras cally change how they recognize words in challenge rela ve to quiet, but that they change in the same ways when confronted with noise or degrada on. 2In addi on, though this work suggests that listeners adopt similar levels of Wait-and-See and Sustained Ac va on across condi ons, it does not fully characterize the degree of stability in the system for two reasons.

text.text: First, the moderate-to-high correla ons that were found reflected different types of challenge.
This may underes mate the overall stability of the system if people's profile is in part driven by a specific response to a specific type of challenge.
Second, tes ng was done on the same day.
This leaves an open ques on as to whether the way word recogni on operates in challenge is stable across me.
That is, do listeners consistently do the same thing in response to challenge, or does it vary by day?
For instance, a first encounter with vocoding might lead to a Wait-and-See profile.
On a subsequent exposure, however, the system might delay very li le but instead show strong Sustained Ac va on.

This could be a form of (unconscious, obligatory) trial-and-error or hypothesis tes ng (a emp ng a new approach that might produce be er results or reduce effort), a natural endogenous change in the system (akin to a circadian rhythm), or even just happenstance.
A more comprehensive approach is needed to test stability across days and across challenge types.

While the work we've discussed thus far focuses on changes to the way that the underlying mechanism operates, in the real world a more important concern in challenging listening is accuracy: Do these changes support (or detract from) people's ability to understand the input?
Previous work has found that the degree to which listeners adopt Wait-and-See and Sustained Ac va on is correlated with how well they perform in tasks of speech-in-noise performance.

In CI users this rela onship is nega ve (McMurray et al., 2024), with greater levels of each dimension leading to worse performance, even a er controlling for the overall quality of the input afforded by each listeners' CI.

text.text: However, an interac on was observed such that each posi vely predicted outcomes in listeners with strong auditory processing speed-listeners who could quickly parse informa on from speech seemed to be able to take advantage of Wait-and-See and Sustained Ac va on.
S ll, there is quite a bit of variance in how well listeners perform in these contexts.
A key missing piece may be differences in how listeners arrive to their idiosyncra c endpoints-the specific changes made in response to challenge.
That is, it may not ma er whether the system becomes more Wait-and-See-or Sustained Ac va on-like, it may be the amount of change rela ve to baseline performance that is important.
Consider a system which might shi recogni on li le to none in response to challenge rela ve to one which might adopt a new approach.

Regardless of the type of change, the strength of this adapta on may predict outcomes-a system which commits to extreme delays or maintenance of compe tors might derive posi ve effects from such shi s in recogni on.
Alterna vely, the magnitude of change might reflect overall ability in these condi ons.
Struggling listeners might shi recogni on much more than those which are successful, in essence searching for a configura on which suits the demands of challenging contexts.
This might predict that increased magnitude of change leads to reduced outcome performance, but the degree of change rela ve to quiet would s ll be of paramount importance.

For a comprehensive picture of how the mechanisms of spoken word recogni on differ in challenging listening, we tested NH listeners on one day in a VWP task with three listening condi ons: Unmanipulated speech in quiet, speech in noise, and vocoded speech.
They were then tested again on the two challenging listening condi ons a week later.

Data from the quiet condi on and the two itera ons of each challenging condi on were then submi ed to a single PCA, to iden fy indices of the degree to which listeners profile of word recogni on exhibit Waitand-See or Sustained Ac va on.
Alongside these VWP experiments, we also examined a variety of individual differences measures as well as standard accuracy measures of speech in several challenging listening condi ons.
These were used to answer three research ques ons.
First, we ask what predicts a listeners' individual profile of word recogni on in challenge.
We considered a range of individual differences factors (e.g., language, cogni ve control, hearing), as well as the effect of day (to test for learning).
Most importantly, we extend previous work by asking if individual differences in word recogni on in challenge are constrained by how a listener recognizes words in quiet.

To the extent that this is observed, this suggests that not only is individual varia on in word recogni on characterized by Sustained Ac va on and Wait-and-See, but that these dimensions constrain the nature of adapta on to challenge-people who are already inclined to recognize words in a certain way tend to adapt in that same way when encountering difficulty.
Second, we ask if the way words are recognized in challenge is stable across me and across challenge types.

We used a commonality analysis to ask how much of the variance in word recogni on in challenge is unique to that type of challenge, unique to listeners' general response on that day, or shared across days and challenge types.
In the same vein, we ask how much of this variance can be a ributed to the profile of word recogni on in quiet vs. the degree that is unique to challenge.
Thus, this inves gates the latent structure of a poten ally muldimensional broader trait of word recogni on in challenging condi ons.
Finally, we ask whether individual differences in the profile of recogni on predict performance in challenging condi ons.
Notably, we include measures of three different kinds of challenging listening performance: Speech-in-noise, vocoded speech, and rapid speech.
Tests of speech-in-noise and vocoded speech are fairly common (and have been used in prior work; Muegge & McMurray, 2025), while tests of how well listeners can parse rapid speech are less so.

text.text: Despite this, rapid speech represents a listening condi on that may be par cularly relevant for Wait-and-See; listeners who delay more might have a harder me comprehending rapid speech, as the informa on passes too quickly for slowed recogni on to keep up.

Moreover, it may be that while an aggressive adop on of Wait-and-See is beneficial for some types of challenge (strongly changing recogni on to a more delayed profile could help in noise or degrada on), it may be par cularly maladap ve in this case.

Cri cally, we use an SEM framework that predicts all three challenging listening condi ons both from the individual differences factors tested for our first research ques on and by the dimensions of spoken word recogni on in challenge iden fied by the PCA, while accoun ng for poten ally shared variance among the outcome measures.
In par cular, we examine the rela onship of a listeners' profile of word recogni on both in absolute terms and in terms the degree of change listeners undergo in challenge rela ve to quiet.
One hundred and eleven par cipants par cipated in this study (ages ranged from 18.1-72.5; mean age = 25.39).
All par cipants followed protocols approved by the par cipa ng university's IRB and either received class credit or $80 for par cipa on.
Par cipants were recruited either through the SONA undergraduate psychology recrui ng portal or through an email sent to the students, faculty, and staff of the university.

Par cipa on was limited to listeners who: (a) had normal or normal-corrected vision; (b) had no history of brain damage or neural disorders; (c) were primarily English-speaking adults with no history of learning an addi onal language from birth; and (d) had age-typical hearing.
This last criterion was confirmed via a hearing screening prior to par cipa on (this same hearing screening was later used as a factor in analyses).
One-hundred and two par cipants returned for their second appointment.
Four par cipants were removed for having missing or incomplete data in the primary VWP task.
We then adopted a set of criteria for addi onal exclusions.

First, a par cipant was dropped from analysis if they had low accuracy in either noise condi on (correctly selec ng the target word < 50% of the me), or if the mecourse func ons were unable to be fit for that par cipant (they did not resemble the standard logis c or asymmetric Gaussian func ons necessary for analysis, see below).

text.text: In addi on, we dropped par cipants who simply did not make a lot of fixa ons (not fixa ng any item on screen on over 50% of trials), as this is likely due to varia on in how a en on and eye-movements are strategically deployed as opposed to meaningful differences in word recogni on.
Given these criteria, we dropped 14 par cipants from the first day and eight par cipants from the second day of VWP results.
The final sample size was 94 for the first day of the VWP and 93 for the second day of the VWP, though only 79 had data from both days.
Seventy-one par cipants completed the en re ba ery of tests.
Analyses which did not require data for all tests (e.g., the PCAs) were performed on all available data points.
For instance, if a par cipant completed both VWP tasks but no other experiments, they were s ll included in the PCA.
Design.
The first and second day of the VWP were iden cal in structure but differed in number of trials and s muli.
Words were assembled into sets of four (see Appendix A for a full list) which were always displayed together.
Each set contained two pairs of cohort compe tors, which were related to each other phone cally but not seman cally.
For instance, a set might contain the words mother, money, lizard, and liver.
Each word in the set was heard as the target s mulus at least once, cycling the roles items played on every trial.
Thus, when the first word was heard (mother) a cohort (money) and two unrelateds (lizard; liver) were on screen.
When the third word was heard (lizard) the fourth became a cohort (liver) and the original pair (mother and money) became unrelated.
Thus, every trial had a target, cohort, and two unrelateds on screen (a TCUU design).
Item sets were assigned to condi on (quiet, noise day 1, vocoding day 2, etc.) such that no item was repeated across condi ons.
Thus, within a par cipant each block of trials had a unique set of items.
This was intended to prevent subjects from learning the precise acous c form of a word in one block (e.g., in quiet) and carrying it over to alter processing in later condi ons (e.g., noise).
Quiet trials contained the same twenty-five sets for all par cipants.
The remaining items were assigned randomly (without replacement) to each of the four subsequent blocks (vocoding day 1/2, noise day 1/2).
Across all blocks the ra o of monosyllabic to bisyllabic sets were controlled, ensuring rough equality (e.g., each block might contain five bisyllabic sets of the total 25).
All subjects started with the quiet block on the first day.
Subsequent blocks were either noise-masked or vocoded, with the order counterbalanced across par cipants.
The second-day VWP began with either noise or vocoding, following the same counterbalancing as day one.
Trials were randomized within a block.

Within a block of trials, each set was cycled through twice, to avoid a process of elimina on strategy-a er hearing the first three items as a target word, listeners could not be sure what the fourth would be.
Across sets, loca on was randomized such that the target word appeared in each loca on an equal number of mes.
With three blocks (quiet, noise, and vocoding), twenty-five sets per block, four words per set, and two repe ons of each word, the first-day VWP contained 600 trials (32542).
The second-day VWP contained 400 trials, as it tested only the noise and vocoding condi ons.
Audio s muli.
S muli were generated via Google's Text to Speech API.
Target words were generated in a neutral carrier sentence ("She said") followed by a pause before the target word.
The target word was then excised from the carrier phrase, cleaned using Praat (Boersma, 2023), and normalized to an amplitude of 70 dB.
text.formatted: The target word was then excised from the carrier phrase, cleaned using Praat <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Boersma, 2023)</ref>, and normalized to an amplitude of 70 dB.

text.text: One hundred milliseconds of silence were added to the onset of each word to ensure a standard s mulus onset.
These base s muli were then manipulated further to create the noise-masked and vocoding condi ons.
For the noise s muli, custom MATLAB code was used to apply speech-shaped noise to each word (noise spectrum was generated based on the average spectrum across all auditory tokens).
Noise began 20 milliseconds a er the beginning of the audio file and ramped up to a peak amplitude of 0.4 over 30 msec.
This was added to the base s mulus (which had varying amplitude, mean = 0.46) for an average signal-to-noise ra o of +1 (signal 1 dB louder than noise).
These procedures replicate those used in Muegge and McMurray (2025), though with a higher level of noise.
text.formatted: These procedures replicate those used in <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Muegge and McMurray (2025)</ref>, though with a higher level of noise.

text.text: For the vocoding s muli, base auditory tokens were processed with AngelSim (Emily Shannon Fu Founda on) using a 5-channel noise processer, Greenwood func on filter, and white noise carrier.
This is again similar to Muegge and McMurray (2025), but with 5-channel vocoding rather than 6.
text.formatted: This is again similar to <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Muegge and McMurray (2025)</ref>, but with 5-channel vocoding rather than 6.

text.text: Visual s muli.
Visual s muli were taken from a database of clipart images, developed and maintained by the lab.
Each image in the database underwent rigorous valida on procedures.
First, mul ple poten al referents were downloaded for a given target.

Next, a focus group made up of members of the lab selected the most prototypical image (or requested new candidates), and provided sugges ons to enhance prototypicality (e.g., by removing background elements, changing color and orienta on of objects, etc.).
Mul ple rounds of these focus groups could occur.
Finally, a senior member of lab who was not involved in the edi ng process gives their approval.
Images are selected and edited in such a way that each image in the database reflects a similar visual style.
Procedure.
Every trial began with four images (one in each corner of the screen) and a center circle which par cipants clicked on to play a word over headphones.
Listeners were tasked with selec ng which image best represented the word they heard.
Pictures were 300 by 300 pixels, displayed on a 5:4 aspect ra o monitor at 1280  1024 resolu on.
Eye-movements were recorded using a SR Research Eyelink 1000 eye tracker, with par cipants placing their heads in a head rest.
Both corneal reflec on and pupil were used for tracking.
A nine-point calibra on procedure was conducted prior to each VWP task.
Dri corrects occurred every 40 trials for the two VWP tasks; failure to pass a dri correct was resolved by recalibra ng the eye tracker.
Alongside the first-and second-day VWP, we included five other tasks.
Audiometry.
Par cipants underwent pure tone audiometry, with intensity thresholds measured at 250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000, and 8000 Hz in each ear using a Grayson Stadler GSI Audiostar Pro audiometer.
This was used to exclude par cipants whose hearing was above clinical thresholds (e.g., 70 dB SPL), though no par cipants reached this criterion.

However, it was also used as an individual differences covariate, as some work suggests that even in normal hearing listeners small differences in sub-clinical hearing ability predict speech in noise performance (Holmes & Griffiths, 2019).
text.formatted: However, it was also used as an individual differences covariate, as some work suggests that even in normal hearing listeners small differences in sub-clinical hearing ability predict speech in noise performance <ref type="bibr">(Holmes & Griffiths, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: To provide an es mate of overall speed of processing (ability to quickly decode and iden fy relevant informa on) and task performance in the VWP (general fixa on speed, or comfort with motor movements required for task comple on), we deployed a non-linguis c version of the VWP (Farris-Trimble & McMurray, 2013).
text.formatted: To provide an es mate of overall speed of processing (ability to quickly decode and iden fy relevant informa on) and task performance in the VWP (general fixa on speed, or comfort with motor movements required for task comple on), we deployed a non-linguis c version of the VWP <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Farris-Trimble & McMurray, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: On each trial, four colored shapes were displayed at the corners of the screen alongside a center circle.
Once the circle turned red, the subject clicked on it to see the target shape. which appeared at the center of the screen for 100 milliseconds.
Par cipants then clicked on its match from among four alterna ves on screen.
As with the auditory VWP, the shapes on each trail cons tuted a set in which pairs were related.
For instance, one set might contain a yellow chevron, a yellow moon, a purple hourglass, and a purple cross.
Thus, every set contained a target, a color compe tor, and two unrelated items (TCUU).
Looks to these items over me capture how quickly listeners can recognize and parse informa on in general (as opposed to language, specifically).
Sixteen total sets were used, each with two color pairs.
Shapes and colors were repeated across sets (e.g., two sets might both contain chevrons or yellow items) but specific shape-color combina ons were not (yellow chevrons were only used once).
The same shapes and colors were not always paired together (yellow and purple were not always together, nor chevrons and moons), but colors were always contras ve within a set.
Shapes and colors were chosen such that they were not easily nameable, to avoid an inadvertent influence of language on performance.
Prototypical hues that remained in the task (e.g. red) were desaturated for the same purpose.
Colors were selected such that par cipants with common kinds of color blindness could complete the task.
Each item in a set appeared as the target three mes, resul ng in 192 trials (1643).
Trials were fully randomized.
Dri correc ons occurred every 32 trials.
Eye-movements were recorded and analyzed throughout the trial similarly to the spoken word VWP (see below).
The spa al Stroop task was used to es mate inhibitory control.
In this task par cipants saw an arrow and responded to its direc on by pressing the le or right arrow keys on a keyboard.

The arrow appeared on either the le or right side of a screen, resul ng in four trial types: an arrow on the le facing le , an arrow on the le facing right, and their respec ve reverse on the right side.

Par cipants tend to respond faster on trials in which the direc on of the arrow and the loca on of the arrow on screen are congruent (e.g., the arrow on the le facing le or the arrow on the right, facing right; a congruent trial) rela ve to when the direc on and loca on mismatch (incongruent trials).
This is thought to be a result of conflict between the relevant (direc on) and irrelevant (loca on) informa on provided on incongruent trials.
Par cipants with stronger cogni ve control can inhibit this irrelevant informa on and are faster when facing incongruent s muli.
The difference in reac on me between congruent and incongruent trials thus acts as an index of cogni ve control.
Par cipants were provided instruc ons and eight prac ce trials prior to beginning the task.
The task consisted of two blocks of 86 trials.
Trials were randomly presented, with the correct direc on (right or le ) appearing an equal number of mes.
However, congruent trials were presented twice as o en as incongruent trials, to suppress training effects.
To assess language ability, par cipants completed the Oral Comprehension subtest from the Woodcock Johson ba ery.
This is administered as a series of sentences whose final word is missing.
Using contextual informa on from the preceding sentence, listeners are asked to fill in this word.
Trials become progressively harder, in both length and vocabulary demands.
As we planned to use this as a measure of individual differences, not as a tool for norming performance to a standard, we did not follow standard stopping and basal rules.
S muli were provided as audio recordings over headphones, with par cipants responding orally.
All par cipants received 15 s muli, from trial 19 (the typical star ng point for adults) to 33 (the final s mulus).
(Ten par cipants instead received 12 trials, from 22 to 33).
Responses were recorded live by an experimenter, then scored post-assessment.
Percent correct served as a measure of language ability.
Speech Percep on Performance.
We measured speech percep on performance in noise, vocoding, and very rapid speech.
These followed a similar structure.
Listeners heard thirty low-context sentences from the IEEE database (Rothauser, 1969), either masked with speech-shaped noise, degraded via vocoding, or sped up to unnaturally fast rates.
text.formatted: Listeners heard thirty low-context sentences from the IEEE database <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Rothauser, 1969)</ref>, either masked with speech-shaped noise, degraded via vocoding, or sped up to unnaturally fast rates.

text.text: Each trial began with a brief warning tone prior to the onset of the s mulus.
Listeners then repeated the sentence back to an examiner, who scored them on how many of five key words they correctly reported.
This was done by selec ng which of the five words were correctly repeated from a list provided on a screen.
Par cipants were turned away from the experimenter as to not receive feedback on their performance.
Sentences were provided in random order, but the set of sentences for each challenge type remained constant.
Noise was always heard first, followed by vocoding, and finally by rapid speech.
S muli genera on followed the same techniques as those used in the VWP task.
The speech-shape noise manipula on remained at an SRN of +1 SNR.
Degrada on was set at 8channel vocoding.
To create the rapid s muli, sentences were sped up 30% of the original rate using PSOLA in Praat.
Following informed consent and the audiogram, par cipants completed the Spa al Stroop and first-day VWP tasks.
On their second visit, listeners performed the second-day VWP, the non-linguis c VWP, the two outcome measures, and the Speeded Sentences task, before ending with Oral Comprehension.
Demographics were collected at the end of the first day.
Audio for all s muli across all tasks were presented over Sennheiser HD 280 PRO headphones via an M-Audio AIR 192|4 amplifier.
Our overall treatment of the data followed previous work (Muegge & McMurray, 2025).
text.formatted: Our overall treatment of the data followed previous work <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Muegge & McMurray, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In brief, a er preprocessing, we computed the looks to the target, cohort and unrelated fixa ons over me in each condi on (quiet, day 1 noise, day 1 vocoding, day 2 noise, and day 2 vocoding).
We then curve-fit each par cipant's performance to describe the pa ern of looking in each condi on with a set of parameters (e.g., target slope, cohort peak).
Next, this set of curve-fit parameters was submi ed to a PCA to iden fy underlying dimensionality.
Finally, we extracted es mates of each PC for each subject as an es mate of how strongly they exhibited a Wait-and-See or Sustained Ac va on profile in that condi on.
Each of these steps are described in detail below.
Eye-tracking Preprocessing.
Eye-tracking data was preprocessed using EyelinkAnalysis (version 5.533; McMurray, 2023).
text.formatted: Eye-tracking data was preprocessed using EyelinkAnalysis <ref type="bibr">(version 5.533;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">McMurray, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: EyelinkAnalysis groups saccades with their subsequent fixa ons into a single look, then computes what item par cipants were looking at on every trial every four milliseconds.
Boundaries around items are ar ficially extended during this process by 150 pixels on all sides, so that looks made around an object are assigned as looks made to that object.
A er pre-processing, but prior to curve-fi ng, we examined overall accuracy as a func on of item.

If at least one of any given target-cohort pair had significantly low accuracy (<70%) across both challenging condi ons, the en re pair was dropped from further analysis. 56 pairs were eventually dropped for failing to meet this criterion.
text.formatted: If at least one of any given target-cohort pair had significantly low accuracy (<70%) across both challenging condi ons, the en re pair was dropped from further analysis. 56 pairs were eventually dropped for failing to meet this criterion.

text.text: Note that since target-cohort pairs were randomly assigned to condi on across subjects, this was not differen ally biased for any condi on.
We next computed average looks across trials made to the target, cohort, and the average across both unrelateds for each par cipant in each condi on.
This excluded trials in which the listener did not correctly iden fy the target.
Curve-fi ng.
Each of these three fixa on curves was then fit with a series of non-linear curves.

Fits were made using custom MATLAB so ware (version 49; McMurray, 2024) which used a constrained gradient descent algorithm to minimize the mean squared error between par cipant's data and the func on while introducing reasonable constraints (e.g., the average looks to the target cannot exceed 1).
For targets, a four-parameter logis c func on was used (Figure 2A).
text.formatted: For targets, a four-parameter logis c func on was used (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2A</ref>).

text.text: This is defined by a Maximum value (the ul mate height of the curve), a Minimum value (the ini al base of the curve), a Slope value (the slope of the curve), and a Crossover point (the me at which the value the curve reaches half its maximum).

Each of these parameters capture different aspects of the mecourse of word recogni on: Maximum provides an es mate of the amount that listeners fixated the target when correctly iden fying it, Minimum provides average baseline fixa ons prior to hearing a word, Slope indicates how quickly listeners fixate the target, and Crossover captures any overall delay in the system.
For cohorts and unrelated items, an asymmetric Gaussian func on was used (Figure 2B).
text.formatted: For cohorts and unrelated items, an asymmetric Gaussian func on was used (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2B</ref>).

text.text: This is defined by six parameters.

This fits the first half of data (before the peak) with half of a Gaussian curve which rises from baseline to peak and the second half with another Gaussian that falls from the same peak back to baseline.
This allows each half to have its own baseline and rate of rise (Figure 2).
text.formatted: This allows each half to have its own baseline and rate of rise (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: These parameters also capture important aspects of word recogni on: Baseline1 again indicates ini al fixa ons prior to hearing a word, Slope1 captures how quickly listeners fixate the cohort, Height the greatest degree to which this cohort is fixated, Mu the point in me where the largest amount of fixa ons occur, Slope2 the rate at which fixa ons to the cohort decay, and finally Baseline2 provides an es mate to what degree listeners con nue to fixate the cohort even a er iden fying the correct target word.
The set of parameters extracted from this curve-fi ng technique describe individual par cipant's profile of fixa ons in a given condi on.
In doing so they can collec vely capture a listener's profile of word recogni on (e.g., Wait-and-See or Sustained Ac va on).
For instance, Wait-and-See is largely defined by delayed target crossover, and delayed cohort looks (Mu) and reduced peak looking.
Similarly, Sustained Ac va on is defined by elevated looks to the cohort late in processing, a reduc on in target Maximum and related increase in cohort Slope2 and Baseline2.
A er curve-fi ng, the fixa ons for each par cipant in each condi on are described by sixteen total parameters (four from the target and six each from the cohort and unrelated curves).
Target Minimum and cohort/unrelated Baseline2 represent fixa ons made prior to hearing any auditory token and thus are irrelevant for word recogni on.
These were removed from analysis, leaving 13 remaining parameters.
We then performed addi onal cleaning.
PCA is highly sensi ve to outliers; to address this, we followed procedures introduced in Muegge and McMurray (2025) to iden fy and impute outliers.
text.formatted: PCA is highly sensi ve to outliers; to address this, we followed procedures introduced in <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Muegge and McMurray (2025)</ref> to iden fy and impute outliers.

text.text: A series of regressions were conducted to predict values in one parameter by values in all others (e.g., predic ng target Maximum by the remaining twelve parameters).
We then removed standardized residuals of greater than or less than ±2.5 (e.g., 2.5 SD from the regression).
In essence, this procedure iden fied individual parameters for individual par cipants which were highly unusual given the rest of the data.
These parameters were then imputed via the mice package in R (van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011).
text.formatted: These parameters were then imputed via the mice package in R (van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011).

text.text: Finally, this imputed data was collated across all condi ons (quiet, noise, and vocoding on day one and two), z-scored, and submi ed to a single PCA. 3 Each condi on for each par cipant was treated as a separate row in the dataset, maximizing the amount of data available and normalizing the resul ng PC space so that performance in each condi on was indexed to the same set of underlying dimensions as all others.
text.formatted: Finally, this imputed data was collated across all condi ons (quiet, noise, and vocoding on day one and two), z-scored, and submi ed to a single PCA. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_2">3</ref> Each condi on for each par cipant was treated as a separate row in the dataset, maximizing the amount of data available and normalizing the resul ng PC space so that performance in each condi on was indexed to the same set of underlying dimensions as all others.

text.text: A er running the PCA, meaningful PCs were selected in a two-step process.
First, PCs with eigenvalues below 1.0 were discarded.
Next, a scree-plot was examined to find the point at which a 'drop off' in the variance explained was observed.
Meaningful PCs were then interpreted using two techniques First, we used their loadings (what parameters each PC was associated with).
For example, if a PC heavily loaded onto target Crossover, cohort Mu, and cohort Height, we interpreted this as a Wait-and-See dimension.
Second, we used a visualiza on process wherein eye-tracking curves were reconstructed from the PCA (outlined in McMurray et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Second, we used a visualiza on process wherein eye-tracking curves were reconstructed from the PCA (outlined in <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">McMurray et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This began by defining high and low values of that component (e.g., 2 SD above and below the mean) and mul plying each loading by that value.
Notably, factor loadings were z-scaled (since the parameters were z-scored prior to the PCA).
We thus used the mean and SD of the original dataset to convert the high and low loadings to their original scale.
These recovered values for each parameter were then used as input to logis c and double-gauss func ons to create predicted fixa on curves.
A er characterizing PCs in this way, we adjusted their scaling.
Whether a PCs scales a posi ve or nega ve direc on is arbitrary (and these are mathema cally iden cal).

Thus, to align direc ons across PCs, we compared reconstructed curves and arbitrarily chose for higher values of the PC to represent greater devia on from the normal profile of recogni on (e.g. more delayed recogni on, higher maintenance of candidates).
This ensured that future analyses shared interpreta on direc on-higher values of each dimension mean stronger Wait-and-See or Sustained Ac va on.
We begin by outlining overall accuracy across condi ons, to document that these were in fact challenging for our par cipants.
We next describe the results of the PCA and iden fy its components.
We then compare the noise and vocoding condi ons to baseline quiet performance to establish the nature of the overall effect of listening challenge on word recogni on dynamics.

Finally, we address each of our research ques ons: (I) are listeners' responses to noise and/or vocoding anchored to recogni on performance in quiet; (II) are they stable in how they respond to challenge across me; and (III) does the degree that listeners change recogni on in response to challenge predict how well they perform in tests of outcome performance (e.g., speech in noise).
Averaged across both days, accuracy was 98.56% for words in quiet, 90.70% for words in noise, and 86.39% for words in vocoding.

Accuracy in each challenging condi on was similar across day: Noise on day 1 and 2 were nearly iden cal (90.63% and 90.78% respec vely), while vocoding on day 1 and 2 differed by a few percentage points (84.42% and 88.35%).
This suggests that the two manipula ons used here were indeed challenging, and that listeners found vocoding the more difficulty of the two.
Despite this, very few listeners were unable to complete the task-of the 14 par cipants dropped during analysis, only six were due to low overall accuracy.
Across condi ons the PCA found four PCs with eigenvalues over 1.0.
These collec vely accounted for 80% of the variance.
Examining the loadings (Table 1), the first PC (PC1) appears to reflect Wait-and-See, being strongly associated with later target Crossover, later cohort Mu, and decreased cohort Height.

text.text: When we examine the reconstructed curves for PC1 (Figure 3A), the first is an almost prototypical reflec on of Wait-and-See with delayed target fixa ons and a delayed and reduced cohort peak.
text.formatted: When we examine the reconstructed curves for PC1 (Figure <ref type="figure">3A</ref>), the first is an almost prototypical reflec on of Wait-and-See with delayed target fixa ons and a delayed and reduced cohort peak.

text.text: The second PC (PC2) most strongly reflects Sustained-Ac va on, with loadings sugges ng decreased target Maximum and elevated cohort Baseline2, but importantly no delay in target Crossover (which was linked to PC1/Wait-and-See).
Visualiza ons (Figure 3B) confirm this, with the dominant pa ern being changes in overall height of the cohort rela ve to the asymptote of the target.
text.formatted: Visualiza ons (Figure <ref type="figure">3B</ref>) confirm this, with the dominant pa ern being changes in overall height of the cohort rela ve to the asymptote of the target.

text.text: While differences in the asymptotes conform to the canonical pa ern of Sustained ac va on seen previously, the differences in the cohort peak do not.
Nonetheless, the strong concordance of the asymptotes to prior work led us to treat this as indica ve of Sustained Ac va on.
PCs 3 and 4-while not the focus of this study-also showed systema c profiles (see Supplement 1).

text.text: Introducing noise to this system changes how it behaves, even if the control parameters are constant; model performance becomes poorer overall.
However, this reduced performance is s ll largely dependent on the original parameters-they s ll dictate the way in which informa on flows through the system, even though this informa on is degraded.

In contrast, we show that the ways in which human listeners approach recogni on in challenge are not completely dependent on how they do so in quiet (though this does contribute significant variance).
This suggests that the underlying parameters determining the system have changed; the way word recogni on behaves in challenge is related to, but different from, how it behaves in quiet.

This in turn argues for a modeling approach in which parameters are free to vary given different contexts-the natural state of the system, then, would be to change how it approaches recogni on in different condi ons, as opposed to assuming a stable unchanging set of parameters.
This is not to point out a limita on of TRACE, specifically.
As men oned, many wellknown models in the literature are similarly built around sta c parameters.
In order to more fully capture human language comprehension, however, it will be necessary for newer endeavors to naturally account for how recogni on changes in response to various factors.
A key goal of the present study was to inves gate how listeners recognize words in challenge.
We show that even in normal hearing listeners this is highly stable, impacted by basic lexical and cogni ve differences, and has some impact on performance.
This has relevance for clinical popula ons, par cularly for CI users and other listeners who face challenge rou nely.

These listeners are defined by adapta on to their implant; they must change how they process informa on a er becoming deaf, and again a er having their hearing restored, taking over a year (or more) of con nuous exposure to their implant before plateauing in speech percep on performance (Blamey et al., 2012; Chang et al., 2010; Hamzavi et al., 2003; Krueger et al., 2008).

text.text: More broadly, we see that the way that processing configures is not uniform; people adopt their own idiosyncra c profile of processing.
Importantly, this is both lawful and robust, stable across challenge types and days, and constrained by their baseline recogni on profiles.
Moreover, we find that shi s in recogni on may be maladap ve, with listeners who respond to challenge by eleva ng the level of compe tor maintenance demonstra ng poorer rapid speech comprehension.
